title: Εἴδωλον
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Dione wipes the ichor from Aphrodite’s hand and the wound heals, while Athena and Hera mock the wounded goddess before Zeus, who smiles and tells Aphrodite to leave war to Ares and Athena. Diomedes, though he knows Apollo is shielding Aeneas, rushes at him three times, and the fourth time Apollo warns him to draw back and remember the gap between gods and men; he gives way. Apollo sets Aeneas down in his temple on Pergamus, where Leto and Artemis heal him, and makes a phantom in his shape, over which Trojans and Achaeans hack at one another’s shields. Apollo then sends Ares to rouse the Trojans, and Ares, in the form of the Thracian leader Acamas, calls on Priam’s sons to save Aeneas. Sarpedon reviles Hector for leaving the fighting to the allies, Hector leaps from his chariot and rallies the Trojans, and the Argives hold their ground. Ares covers the battle in night at Apollo’s bidding, since Athena has gone, and Apollo brings Aeneas back out of the sanctuary and puts might in him; his companions are glad to see him whole, and no one has time to ask him anything.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα καὶ ἀμφοτέρῃσιν ἀπ’ ἰχῶ χειρὸς ὀμόργνυ·
sentences.tr: ē rha kai amphoterēisin ap’ ichō cheiros omorgny·
sentences.l: She spoke, and with both hands wiped the ichor from the hand;
sentences.i: So she said, and with both hands wiped the ichor from the hand;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί closes a speech and starts the action, ‘she spoke, and’; the speaker is Dione, who has just finished speaking to Aphrodite in the last part, though the Greek names no one. ἰχῶ is the accusative of ἰχώρ ‘ichor’, the blood of the gods (see 5.340), and ἀπ’ … ὀμόργνυ is tmesis for ἀπομόργνυμι ‘wipe off’, an imperfect without the augment (Attic ἀπωμόργνυ). ἀμφοτέρῃσιν is the dative plural feminine ‘with both’, with χερσίν ‘hands’ understood; χειρός ‘the hand’ is the wounded hand, a genitive of separation. A new paragraph begins at 416.

sentences.t: ἄλθετο χείρ, ὀδύναι δὲ κατηπιόωντο βαρεῖαι.
sentences.tr: altheto cheir, odynai de katēpioōnto bareiai.
sentences.l: healed was the hand, and the pains were being soothed, the heavy ones.
sentences.i: The hand was healed, and the heavy pains were soothed.
sentences.n: ἄλθετο is the imperfect middle of ἄλθομαι ‘get well, be healed’, without the augment. κατηπιόωντο is the imperfect passive of a verb meaning ‘soothe’ (built on ἤπιος ‘gentle’), with the stretched, uncontracted ending -όωντο (Attic -οῦντο), so ‘were being soothed’. ὀδύναι ‘pains’ and βαρεῖαι ‘heavy’ agree. The Greek names no cure but the wiping.

sentences.t:
αἳ δ’ αὖτ’ εἰσορόωσαι Ἀθηναίη τε καὶ Ἥρη
κερτομίοις ἐπέεσσι Δία Κρονίδην ἐρέθιζον.
sentences.tr:
hai d’ aut’ eisoroōsai Athēnaiē te kai Hērē
kertomiois epeessi Dia Kronidēn erethizon.
sentences.l:
But those two in their turn, looking on, Athena and Hera,
with taunting words were provoking Zeus the son-of-Cronus.
sentences.i: But Athena and Hera, who were watching, in their turn provoked Zeus, the son of Cronus, with taunting words.
sentences.n: αἳ δ’ αὖτ’ is ‘but they in turn’ (αἵ, the article as a pronoun, and αὖτε ‘in turn’), passing from Aphrodite to the two goddesses who are watching, named in the apposition Ἀθηναίη … καὶ Ἥρη (Ἀθηναίη is the epic form of Ἀθηνᾶ). εἰσορόωσαι is the uncontracted participle of εἰσοράω ‘look on’. κερτομίοις ἐπέεσσι ‘with taunting words’ is a dative of means, with κερτόμιος the adjective of κερτομέω ‘taunt’; Δία Κρονίδην is ‘Zeus, the son of Cronus’ (Κρονίδης is the patronymic); ἐρέθιζον is the imperfect of ἐρεθίζω ‘provoke’, ‘were provoking’.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: toisi de mythōn ērche thea glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l: And among them of speeches made-beginning the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: The goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε is a stock introduction, ‘and among them was the first to speak’: τοῖσι is ‘among them’, the watching gods, and ἦρχε is the imperfect of ἄρχω, which takes the genitive μύθων ‘speeches’. The same line stands in the Odyssey, and the English is that one. γλαυκῶπις ‘gleaming-eyed’ is Athena’s stock epithet, translated every time; its exact sense is not certain.

sentences.t: Ζεῦ πάτερ ἦ ῥά τί μοι κεχολώσεαι ὅττι κεν εἴπω;
sentences.tr: Zeu pater ē rha ti moi kecholōseai hotti ken eipō;
sentences.l: “Zeus father, can it be that you will be at all angry with me at whatever I may say?
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, will you be at all angry with me for whatever I say?
sentences.n: Ζεῦ πάτερ ‘Zeus father’ is the usual form of address. ἦ ῥά opens a question, ‘can it be that…?’. κεχολώσεαι is the future perfect middle of χολόομαι ‘be angry’ (from χόλος ‘anger’), with the epic ending -εαι (Attic -ῃ), and τι is adverbial, ‘at all’. ὅττι κεν εἴπω is ὅ τι κε(ν) εἴπω, ‘whatever I may say’: the relative ὅ τι with κεν and the aorist subjunctive. Athena asks leave before she mocks.

sentences.t:
ἦ μάλα δή τινα Κύπρις Ἀχαιϊάδων ἀνιεῖσα
Τρωσὶν ἅμα σπέσθαι, τοὺς νῦν ἔκπαγλα φίλησε,
τῶν τινα καρρέζουσα Ἀχαιϊάδων ἐϋπέπλων
πρὸς χρυσῇ περόνῃ καταμύξατο χεῖρα ἀραιήν.
sentences.tr:
ē mala dē tina Kypris Achaiïadōn anieisa
Trōsin hama spesthai, tous nyn ekpagla philēse,
tōn tina karrezousa Achaiïadōn eÿpeplōn
pros chrysēi peronēi katamyxato cheira araiēn.
sentences.l:
Surely indeed Cypris, urging on one of the Achaean women
to follow along with the Trojans, whom now she terribly loved,
and stroking one of those Achaean women, fair-robed,
scratched on a golden brooch her slender hand.”
sentences.i: Surely Cypris, urging one of the Achaean women to follow the Trojans, whom she has now come to love terribly, has scratched her slender hand on a golden brooch while stroking one of those fair-robed Achaean women.”
sentences.n: Athena’s jibe is that Aphrodite was hurt at her own work, urging Achaean women to follow the Trojans. Κύπρις ‘Cypris’ is Aphrodite; Ἀχαιϊάδων is the genitive plural of Ἀχαιϊάς ‘Achaean woman’. ἀνιεῖσα is the participle of ἀνίημι ‘urge on’, with the infinitive σπέσθαι (aorist of ἕπομαι ‘follow’) and ἅμα ‘along with’ the dative Τρωσίν. ἔκπαγλα is the adverb ‘terribly’ and φίλησε the aorist of φιλέω ‘love’, with νῦν ‘now’. καρρέζουσα is a shortened form of καταρρέζω ‘stroke’ (the verb of κατέρεξεν, 1.361); the explanation is the usual one, not a certain one. ἐϋπέπλων ‘fair-robed’ (ἐΰ- ‘well, fair’ + πέπλος ‘robe’) is a stock epithet of women, translated every time and rendered as in the Odyssey, and keeps its printed diaeresis. καταμύξατο is the aorist middle of a verb for ‘scratch’ (καταμύσσω), with πρὸς χρυσῇ περόνῃ ‘against a golden brooch’ and χεῖρα ἀραιήν ‘her slender hand’ (ἀραιός ‘thin, slight’).

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, μείδησεν δὲ πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε,
καί ῥα καλεσσάμενος προσέφη χρυσῆν Ἀφροδίτην·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, meidēsen de patēr andrōn te theōn te,
kai rha kalessamenos prosephē chrysēn Aphroditēn·
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and smiled the father of men and of gods,
and, calling her to himself, addressed golden Aphrodite:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and the father of men and of gods smiled, and, calling golden Aphrodite to him, said to her:
sentences.n: The father of men and of gods is Zeus, named only by his stock phrase, and he smiles at Athena’s jibe. ὣς φάτο ‘so she spoke’ closes Athena’s speech. καλεσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of καλέω ‘call’, with the doubled σ of the epic form, ‘calling to himself’; καί ῥα is ‘and then’, and προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘address’. χρυσῆν Ἀφροδίτην ‘golden Aphrodite’ is the goddess’s stock epithet, translated every time. A new paragraph begins at 426.

sentences.t:
οὔ τοι τέκνον ἐμὸν δέδοται πολεμήϊα ἔργα,
ἀλλὰ σύ γ’ ἱμερόεντα μετέρχεο ἔργα γάμοιο,
ταῦτα δ’ Ἄρηϊ θοῷ καὶ Ἀθήνῃ πάντα μελήσει.
sentences.tr:
ou toi teknon emon dedotai polemēïa erga,
alla sy g’ himeroenta metercheo erga gamoio,
tauta d’ Arēï thoōi kai Athēnēi panta melēsei.
sentences.l:
“Not to you, my child, have the works of war been given,
but do you go after the works of marriage, full of longing,
and these things will all be a care to swift Ares and Athena.”
sentences.i: “The works of war, my child, have not been given to you; go after the works of marriage, full of longing, and these things will all be the care of swift Ares and Athena.”
sentences.n: Zeus’s answer is gentle: war is not Aphrodite’s work. τοι is σοι ‘to you’, τέκνον ἐμόν ‘my child’ (τέκνον is ‘child’, not ‘son’), δέδοται the perfect passive of δίδωμι ‘have been given’, and πολεμήϊα ἔργα ‘the works of war’ (πολεμήϊος ‘of war’). σύ γ’ … μετέρχεο is ‘you at least, go after’: the imperative of μετέρχομαι ‘go after, attend to’, with the epic ending -εο. ἱμερόεντα ‘full of longing’ (ἵμερος ‘longing’ + -όεις ‘full of’) goes with ἔργα γάμοιο ‘the works of marriage’ (epic genitive in -οιο). ταῦτα ‘these things’ are the works of war, and μελήσει ‘will be a care’ takes the dative Ἄρηϊ θοῷ καὶ Ἀθήνῃ ‘swift Ares and Athena’.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἳ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον,
Αἰνείᾳ δ’ ἐπόρουσε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης,
γιγνώσκων ὅ οἱ αὐτὸς ὑπείρεχε χεῖρας Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.tr:
hōs hoi men toiauta pros allēlous agoreuon,
Aineiāi d’ eporouse boēn agathos Diomēdēs,
gignōskōn ho hoi autos hypeireche cheiras Apollōn·
sentences.i: So they spoke such words to one another, and Diomedes, good at the war-cry, rushed upon Aeneas, knowing that Apollo himself was holding his hands over him;
sentences.n: The first line is a repeat of the one at 5.274; the scene now turns from the gods to the fighting. Αἰνείᾳ … ἐπόρουσε is ‘rushed upon Aeneas’ (ἐπόρουσε, aorist of ἐπορούω, with the dative). βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is Diomedes’ stock epithet, translated every time. ὅ is the neuter relative used as ‘that’ (= ὅτι) after γιγνώσκων ‘knowing’; οἱ is ‘over him’, Aeneas; αὐτός is Apollo ‘himself’, in person; and ὑπείρεχε is the imperfect of ὑπερέχω with χεῖρας ‘hands’. To hold one’s hands over a man is to shield him. A new paragraph begins at 431.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅ γ’ ἄρ’ οὐδὲ θεὸν μέγαν ἅζετο, ἵετο δ’ αἰεὶ
Αἰνείαν κτεῖναι καὶ ἀπὸ κλυτὰ τεύχεα δῦσαι.
sentences.tr:
all’ ho g’ ar’ oude theon megan hazeto, hieto d’ aiei
Aineian kteinai kai apo klyta teuchea dysai.
sentences.l:
But he, then, did not even revere the great god, and was always eager
to kill Aeneas and to strip off the famous armour.
sentences.i: But he had no awe even of the great god, and was always eager to kill Aeneas and strip him of his famous armour.
sentences.n: ὅ γε ‘he’ is Diomedes, and γε sets him against the god’s protection. ἅζετο is the imperfect of ἅζομαι ‘stand in awe of, revere’, with οὐδέ ‘not even’; the great god is Apollo. ἵετο is the imperfect middle of ἵημι ‘be eager’, with the infinitive κτεῖναι ‘to kill’ (aorist of κτείνω). ἀπὸ … δῦσαι is tmesis for ἀποδῦσαι, the aorist infinitive of ἀποδύω ‘strip off’, here transitive, ‘strip the armour from him’; κλυτὰ τεύχεα ‘famous armour’ is the Odyssey’s phrase for it.

sentences.t:
τρὶς μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἐπόρουσε κατακτάμεναι μενεαίνων,
τρὶς δέ οἱ ἐστυφέλιξε φαεινὴν ἀσπίδ’ Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.tr:
tris men epeit’ eporouse kataktamenai meneainōn,
tris de hoi estyphelixe phaeinēn aspid’ Apollōn·
sentences.l:
Three times then he rushed on, raging to kill him,
and three times his shining shield Apollo thrust back;
sentences.i: Three times he rushed on, raging to kill him, and three times Apollo drove back his shining shield;
sentences.n: τρὶς μέν … τρὶς δέ sets the two halves of each charge against each other: the mortal rushes, the god strikes his shield back. ἐπόρουσε ‘rushed on’ is the verb of 432. κατακτάμεναι is the aorist infinitive of κατακτείνω ‘kill’ with the epic ending -μεναι (Attic -ναι), and μενεαίνων is the participle of μενεαίνω ‘be furiously eager, rage’. οἱ is the dative of Diomedes (‘his shield’), and ἐστυφέλιξε is the aorist of στυφελίζω ‘strike hard, thrust’ (the verb of 1.581), here a god beating a mortal’s shield away; the Greek does not say how.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τὸ τέταρτον ἐπέσσυτο δαίμονι ἶσος,
δεινὰ δ’ ὁμοκλήσας προσέφη ἑκάεργος Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē to tetarton epessyto daimoni isos,
deina d’ homoklēsas prosephē hekaergos Apollōn·
sentences.l:
But when for the fourth time he rushed on, equal to a divinity,
and dreadfully having shouted at him, addressed him far-working Apollo:
sentences.i: But when he rushed on for the fourth time, like a divinity, Apollo, who works from afar, shouted dreadfully at him and said:
sentences.n: τὸ τέταρτον ‘the fourth time’ completes the count begun at 436. ἐπέσσυτο is the aorist middle of ἐπισεύομαι ‘rush upon’, built on σεύω ‘drive’, with the doubled σ of the epic form. δαίμονι ἶσος ‘equal to a divinity’ is a formula (the same words come at 459); δαίμων here is a divine being. δεινά is a neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘dreadfully’; ὁμοκλήσας is the aorist participle of ὁμοκλάω ‘shout at’, in threat or rebuke; and προσέφη is ‘addressed’. The stock epithet ἑκάεργος ‘far-working’ is translated every time; its meaning is disputed.

sentences.t:
φράζεο Τυδεΐδη καὶ χάζεο, μηδὲ θεοῖσιν
ἶσ’ ἔθελε φρονέειν, ἐπεὶ οὔ ποτε φῦλον ὁμοῖον
ἀθανάτων τε θεῶν χαμαὶ ἐρχομένων τ’ ἀνθρώπων.
sentences.tr:
phrazeo Tydeïdē kai chazeo, mēde theoisin
is’ ethele phroneein, epei ou pote phylon homoion
athanatōn te theōn chamai erchomenōn t’ anthrōpōn.
sentences.l:
“Take heed, Tydeus’-son, and draw back, and do not
equally with gods wish to think, for never is the tribe alike
of immortal gods and of men going upon the ground.”
sentences.i: “Take care, son of Tydeus, and draw back; do not wish to think yourself the equal of gods, since the tribe of the immortal gods is never the same as that of men who walk on the ground.”
sentences.n: Apollo’s warning rests on two imperatives, φράζεο ‘take heed’ (from φράζομαι) and χάζεο ‘draw back’ (from χάζομαι), both with the epic ending -εο (Attic -ου). Τυδεΐδη is the vocative of Τυδεΐδης ‘son of Tydeus’. μηδέ … ἔθελε φρονέειν is a negative command, ‘do not wish to think’; ἶσα is a neuter plural adverb, ‘equally’, with the dative θεοῖσιν ‘with gods’, and φρονέειν has the uncontracted ending -έειν. φῦλον ‘tribe’ is the word for a kind or race, with ὁμοῖον ‘alike’, and the genitives ἀθανάτων τε θεῶν … ἀνθρώπων depend on it. χαμαὶ ἐρχομένων ‘going on the ground’ sets mortals at the level of the earth.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Τυδεΐδης δ’ ἀνεχάζετο τυτθὸν ὀπίσσω
μῆνιν ἀλευάμενος ἑκατηβόλου Ἀπόλλωνος.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, Tydeïdēs d’ anechazeto tytthon opissō
mēnin aleuamenos hekatēbolou Apollōnos.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Tydeus’-son drew back a little, backward,
avoiding the wrath of far-shooting Apollo.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the son of Tydeus drew back a little way, avoiding the wrath of Apollo, who shoots from afar.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ closes Apollo’s speech, and Diomedes obeys. ἀνεχάζετο is the imperfect of ἀναχάζομαι ‘draw back’ (the verb of χάζεο above, with ἀνα- ‘back’), with τυτθόν ‘a little’ and ὀπίσσω ‘backward’ as adverbs. ἀλευάμενος is the aorist participle of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’ (a by-form ἀλεύομαι), and ἑκατηβόλου ‘far-shooting’ is the Odyssey’s epithet of Apollo, translated every time. A new paragraph begins at 443.

sentences.t:
Αἰνείαν δ’ ἀπάτερθεν ὁμίλου θῆκεν Ἀπόλλων
Περγάμῳ εἰν ἱερῇ, ὅθι οἱ νηός γε τέτυκτο.
sentences.tr:
Aineian d’ apaterthen homilou thēken Apollōn
Pergamōi ein hierēi, hothi hoi nēos ge tetykto.
sentences.l:
And Aeneas apart from the throng set down Apollo
in sacred Pergamus, where for him a temple had been built.
sentences.i: And Apollo set Aeneas down away from the throng in sacred Pergamus, where a temple had been built for him.
sentences.n: ἀπάτερθεν ‘apart from’ takes the genitive ὁμίλου ‘the throng’, the crowd of fighters; Apollo has carried Aeneas out of the battle. Περγάμῳ is the dative of Πέργαμος (Latin Pergamus), the citadel of Troy; εἰν is a form of ἐν ‘in’. The temple (νηός, Attic ναός) is Apollo’s own: οἱ is the dative ‘for him’, and τέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω ‘make’. ὅθι is ‘where’.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι τὸν Λητώ τε καὶ Ἄρτεμις ἰοχέαιρα
ἐν μεγάλῳ ἀδύτῳ ἀκέοντό τε κύδαινόν τε·
sentences.tr:
ētoi ton Lētō te kai Artemis iocheaira
en megalōi adytōi akeonto te kydainon te·
sentences.l:
Now him Leto and Artemis, the arrow-pourer,
in the great inner sanctuary were healing and were making glorious;
sentences.i: Now Leto and Artemis, who showers her arrows, healed him in the great inner sanctuary and made him glorious;
sentences.n: ἤτοι (printed as one word) is ‘now, for his part’, and sets what the women of Apollo’s family do against what Apollo does next (αὐτάρ, 449). Λητώ is Leto, mother of Apollo and Artemis; Ἄρτεμις ἰοχέαιρα ‘Artemis, who showers her arrows’ is her stock epithet, translated every time (the second half of the word is disputed in antiquity). ἀδύτῳ is the dative of ἄδυτον ‘inner sanctuary’, the part of a temple not to be entered (ἀ- + δύω ‘enter’). ἀκέοντο is the imperfect middle of ἀκέομαι ‘heal’, unaugmented and uncontracted (Attic ἠκοῦντο), and κύδαινον the imperfect of κυδαίνω ‘make glorious’ (from κῦδος ‘glory’); the Greek says no more than that, and we read it as restoring his splendour.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ εἴδωλον τεῦξ’ ἀργυρότοξος Ἀπόλλων
αὐτῷ τ’ Αἰνείᾳ ἴκελον καὶ τεύχεσι τοῖον,
sentences.tr:
autar ho eidōlon teux’ argyrotoxos Apollōn
autōi t’ Aineiāi ikelon kai teuchesi toion,
sentences.l:
But he a phantom fashioned, silver-bowed Apollo,
like Aeneas himself and such in armour,
sentences.i: But silver-bowed Apollo made a phantom, like Aeneas himself and just like him in armour,
sentences.n: The sentence goes on in the next unit. αὐτάρ ‘but’ and ὅ ‘he’ (Apollo) set the god’s act against what the women did. εἴδωλον ‘phantom’ is an image without substance; τεῦξ’ is the aorist of τεύχω ‘make’, without the augment. ἀργυρότοξος ‘silver-bowed’ is Apollo’s stock epithet, translated every time. ἴκελον ‘like’ agrees with εἴδωλον and takes the dative αὐτῷ … Αἰνείᾳ ‘Aeneas himself’; τεύχεσι τοῖον is ‘such in armour’, that is, equipped as he was (τεύχεα ‘armour’).

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ εἰδώλῳ Τρῶες καὶ δῖοι Ἀχαιοὶ
δῄουν ἀλλήλων ἀμφὶ στήθεσσι βοείας
ἀσπίδας εὐκύκλους λαισήϊά τε πτερόεντα.
sentences.tr:
amphi d’ ar’ eidōlōi Trōes kai dioi Achaioi
dēioun allēlōn amphi stēthessi boeias
aspidas eukyklous laisēïa te pteroenta.
sentences.l:
and around the phantom Trojans and heavenly Achaeans
were hacking at one another’s chests the ox-hide
shields, well-rounded, and the light shields, winged.
sentences.i: and around the phantom the Trojans and the heavenly Achaeans hacked at the ox-hide, well-rounded shields on one another’s chests, and at the winged light shields.
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ εἰδώλῳ is ‘and around the phantom’, the phantom of the unit before. δῄουν is the imperfect of δηϊόω ‘cut down, hack at’, without the augment (Attic ἐδῄουν); ἀλλήλων ἀμφὶ στήθεσσι is ‘on one another’s chests’ (στήθεσσι is the epic dative plural). βοείας ‘of ox-hide’ and εὐκύκλους ‘well-rounded’ (ἐΰ- ‘well’ + κύκλος ‘circle’) go with ἀσπίδας ‘shields’. λαισήϊα is a kind of shield, probably a light one, whose exact kind is not known; πτερόεντα ‘winged’ is the epithet of words and arrows, and what it means of shields is not known (perhaps light, or fluttering). Trojans and Achaeans fight over a shape with no man in it.

sentences.t: δὴ τότε θοῦρον Ἄρηα προσηύδα Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.tr: dē tote thouron Arēa prosēuda Phoibos Apollōn·
sentences.l: Then indeed to impetuous Ares spoke Phoebus Apollo:
sentences.i: Then Phoebus Apollo spoke to impetuous Ares:
sentences.n: δὴ τότε ‘then indeed’ marks the moment when Apollo turns from the phantom to the war-god. θοῦρον Ἄρηα is the accusative (Ἄρηα is an epic accusative of Ἄρης) with the stock epithet θοῦρος ‘impetuous’, translated every time; Ares is the god here, not ‘war’. προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’, which takes the accusative of the person spoken to; Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων ‘Phoebus Apollo’ is the god with his title.

sentences.l:
“Ares, Ares, mortal-ruining, blood-stained, wall-stormer,
would you not now draw this man out of the fight, having gone after him,
Tydeus’-son, who now would fight even with father Zeus?
sentences.i: “Ares, Ares, ruin of mortals, blood-stained, stormer of walls, will you not go and draw this man out of the fight, the son of Tydeus, who by now would fight even with father Zeus?
sentences.n: The first line is Athena’s address to Ares at 5.31, translated as it was there; Apollo borrows the form of address, which names the god by what he does. Ἆρες Ἄρες is a doubled vocative; βροτολοιγέ ‘ruin of mortals’ (βροτός ‘mortal’ + λοιγός ‘ruin’), μιαιφόνε ‘blood-stained’ (the second part is φόνος ‘killing’), τειχεσιπλῆτα ‘stormer of walls’ (the second part is disputed: πελάζω ‘approach’ or πλήσσω ‘strike’). οὐκ ἂν δή … ἐρύσαιο is a request in the form of a question, ‘would you not draw…?’: ἐρύσαιο is the aorist optative middle of ἐρύω ‘draw’, with μάχης ‘from the fight’ (genitive of separation) and μετελθών ‘going after him’. The man is τόνδ’ … Τυδεΐδην ‘this man, the son of Tydeus’. ὃς … μάχοιτο is a relative clause with the optative and ἄν, ‘who would fight’, and Διὶ πατρί ‘father Zeus’ is the dative after it.

sentences.t:
Κύπριδα μὲν πρῶτα σχεδὸν οὔτασε χεῖρ’ ἐπὶ καρπῷ,
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ’ αὐτῷ μοι ἐπέσσυτο δαίμονι ἶσος.
sentences.tr:
Kyprida men prōta schedon outase cheir’ epi karpōi,
autar epeit’ autōi moi epessyto daimoni isos.
sentences.l:
Cypris, on the one hand, first at close quarters he wounded, the hand at the wrist,
but then upon me myself he rushed, equal to a divinity.”
sentences.i: He wounded Cypris first, at close quarters, in the hand at the wrist, and then he rushed upon me myself, like a divinity.”
sentences.n: Κύπριδα μέν … αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα sets the first wound against the attack on Apollo himself. Κύπριδα is the accusative of Κύπρις ‘Cypris’ (Aphrodite); σχεδόν is ‘near, at close quarters’; οὔτασε is the aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound’; and χεῖρ’ ἐπὶ καρπῷ is ‘the hand at the wrist’ (the hand is an accusative of the part wounded, καρπός ‘wrist’). αὐτῷ μοι is ‘upon me myself’, αὐτῷ agreeing with the dative μοι after ἐπέσσυτο ‘rushed upon’ (see 438); δαίμονι ἶσος is the formula of 438.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν αὐτὸς μὲν ἐφέζετο Περγάμῳ ἄκρῃ,
Τρῳὰς δὲ στίχας οὖλος Ἄρης ὄτρυνε μετελθὼν
εἰδόμενος Ἀκάμαντι θοῷ ἡγήτορι Θρῃκῶν·
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn autos men ephezeto Pergamōi akrēi,
Trōias de stichas oulos Arēs otryne metelthōn
eidomenos Akamanti thoōi hēgētori Thrēikōn·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and sat down himself on high Pergamus, while ruinous Ares went among the Trojan ranks and urged them on, making himself like swift Acamas, leader of the Thracians;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ ends Apollo’s speech and starts his move; αὐτός is Apollo ‘himself’, set against Ares (μὲν … δέ). ἐφέζετο is the imperfect of ἐφέζομαι ‘sit down on’, with the dative Περγάμῳ ἄκρῃ ‘on high Pergamus’ (ἄκρος ‘high, topmost’), the citadel of 446. οὖλος Ἄρης ‘ruinous Ares’: οὖλος is ‘baneful, ruinous’, related to οὐλομένην (1.2), and is translated every time; the Iliad’s other epithet of Ares is θοῦρος ‘impetuous’ (454). Τρῳάς is the adjective ‘Trojan’; ὄτρυνε is the past tense of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, without the augment (ὤτρυνε), and μετελθών ‘going among them’. εἰδόμενος is the present participle of εἴδομαι ‘be like, seem like’, so ‘making himself like’: the god takes the shape of Acamas, ἡγήτωρ ‘leader’ of the Θρῃκῶν ‘Thracians’ (genitive plural). A new paragraph begins at 460.

sentences.t: υἱάσι δὲ Πριάμοιο διοτρεφέεσσι κέλευεν·
sentences.tr: huiasi de Priamoio diotrepheessi keleuen·
sentences.l: and the Zeus-nurtured sons of Priam he bade:
sentences.i: and he bade the Zeus-nurtured sons of Priam:
sentences.n: κέλευεν is the imperfect of κελεύω ‘bid’, here with the dative υἱάσι (an epic dative plural of υἱός) ‘the sons’, and the colon points to the words of the order, which follow. διοτρεφέεσσι ‘Zeus-nurtured’ (Διός + τρέφω ‘nourish’) is a stock epithet of kings and their houses, translated every time; it comes again in the next line. Ares is still speaking in the shape of Acamas (462).

sentences.t:
ὦ υἱεῖς Πριάμοιο διοτρεφέος βασιλῆος
ἐς τί ἔτι κτείνεσθαι ἐάσετε λαὸν Ἀχαιοῖς;
sentences.tr:
ō huieis Priamoio diotrepheos basilēos
es ti eti kteinesthai easete laon Achaiois;
sentences.l:
“O sons of Priam, the Zeus-nurtured king,
to what point still will you allow the people to be killed by the Achaeans?
sentences.i: “Sons of Priam, the Zeus-nurtured king, how long will you go on letting the troops be killed by the Achaeans?
sentences.n: ὦ υἱεῖς: ὦ is the vocative particle and υἱεῖς the plural of υἱός. Πριάμοιο διοτρεφέος βασιλῆος is ‘of Priam, the Zeus-nurtured king’ (epic genitives in -οιο and -ῆος, Attic -ου and -έως). ἐς τί ἔτι is ‘to what point still’, that is, ‘how long’; ἐάσετε is the future of ἐάω ‘allow’, with the passive infinitive κτείνεσθαι ‘to be killed’ and the dative of the agent Ἀχαιοῖς ‘by the Achaeans’; λαόν ‘the people’ is the Trojan army. The speaker is Ares in disguise.

sentences.t: ἦ εἰς ὅ κεν ἀμφὶ πύλῃς εὖ ποιητῇσι μάχωνται;
sentences.tr: ē eis ho ken amphi pylēis eu poiētēisi machōntai;
sentences.l: Or is it until they fight about the well-made gates?
sentences.i: Will you let it go on until they are fighting around the well-built gates?
sentences.n: ἦ opens a second question that continues the first. εἰς ὅ κεν … μάχωνται is ‘until they fight’: εἰς ὅ κεν is ‘until’, with the subjunctive. πύλῃς is the epic dative plural of πύλη, ‘gates’, and εὖ ποιητῇσι ‘well-made’ (ποιητός, from ποιέω ‘make’) is the epic dative plural -ῃσι; the gates are those of the city. The English takes its verb from the question before.

sentences.t:
κεῖται ἀνὴρ ὃν ἶσον ἐτίομεν Ἕκτορι δίῳ
Αἰνείας υἱὸς μεγαλήτορος Ἀγχίσαο·
sentences.tr:
keitai anēr hon ison etiomen Hektori diōi
Aineias huios megalētoros Anchisao·
sentences.l:
There lies a man whom we honoured equally with heavenly Hector,
Aeneas, son of great-spirited Anchises;
sentences.i: A man lies there whom we honoured as we honoured heavenly Hector, Aeneas, son of great-spirited Anchises;
sentences.n: κεῖται ἀνήρ ‘a man lies’ opens the report of Aeneas’ fall; the name comes only in the next line, Αἰνείας, nominative in apposition to ἀνήρ. ὃν ἶσον ἐτίομεν Ἕκτορι δίῳ is ‘whom we honoured equally with heavenly Hector’: ἶσον is an adverb, ἐτίομεν the imperfect of τίω ‘honour’, and δίῳ the dative of δῖος ‘heavenly’. μεγαλήτορος ‘great-spirited’ (μέγας + ἦτορ ‘heart’) is the epithet of Anchises. Line 468 is metrically irregular as transmitted: its fifth foot is a spondee (Ἀγ-χῑ́), because the ι of Ἀγχίσαο has to be long for the line to fill six feet, and the sixth foot σᾱ-ο needs the α before the final -ο to count as long (the scansion marks it as lengthened).

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’ ἐκ φλοίσβοιο σαώσομεν ἐσθλὸν ἑταῖρον.
sentences.tr: all’ aget’ ek phloisboio saōsomen esthlon hetairon.
sentences.l: but come, out of the roar let us save the good companion.”
sentences.i: But come, let us save our good companion out of the roar of battle.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγετε ‘but come’ (plural) rallies the princes. σαώσομεν is a first person plural aorist subjunctive, with the short vowel of the epic subjunctive, ‘let us save’. ἐκ φλοίσβοιο is ‘out of the roar’: φλοῖσβος is the loud noise of battle (the root of πολυφλοίσβοιο ‘loud-roaring’, 1.34). ἐσθλὸν ἑταῖρον ‘the good companion’ is Aeneas. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὄτρυνε μένος καὶ θυμὸν ἑκάστου.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn otryne menos kai thymon hekastou.
sentences.l: So having spoken, he urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ ends the speech. ὄτρυνε ‘urged on’ is the past tense of ὀτρύνω, without the augment (ὤτρυνε), with two objects, μένος ‘might’ and θυμόν ‘heart’, the pair that make a man’s fighting spirit; ἑκάστου ‘of each’ is a possessive genitive, ‘the might and heart of each man’. A new paragraph begins at 470.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ αὖ Σαρπηδὼν μάλα νείκεσεν Ἕκτορα δῖον·
sentences.tr: enth’ au Sarpēdōn mala neikesen Hektora dion·
sentences.l: Then in turn Sarpedon greatly reviled heavenly Hector:
sentences.i: Then Sarpedon, in his turn, reviled heavenly Hector sharply:
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ αὖ is ‘then in turn’, handing the story from Ares to Sarpedon, who in his speech calls himself an ally (478). νείκεσεν is the aorist of νεικέω ‘revile’ (the verb of νεῖκος ‘quarrel’), with the object Ἕκτορα δῖον ‘heavenly Hector’, and μάλα ‘greatly’ strengthens it; the colon points to the reproach that follows.

sentences.t: Ἕκτορ πῇ δή τοι μένος οἴχεται ὃ πρὶν ἔχεσκες;
sentences.tr: Hektor pēi dē toi menos oichetai ho prin echeskes;
sentences.l: “Hector, where indeed has your might gone, which you used to have before?
sentences.i: “Hector, where has your might gone, which you used to have before?
sentences.n: μένος ‘might’ is the fighting strength Sarpedon accuses Hector of having lost. πῇ δή τοι … οἴχεται is ‘where indeed has … gone’ (πῇ ‘where’, οἴχεται the present of οἴχομαι ‘be gone’, with the sense of a perfect), and τοι is σοι ‘your’, a dative of possession. ὃ πρὶν ἔχεσκες is ‘which before you used to have’: ὅ is the neuter relative and ἔχεσκες an iterative imperfect, the suffix -σκ- marking a habit.

sentences.t:
φῆς που ἄτερ λαῶν πόλιν ἑξέμεν ἠδ’ ἐπικούρων
οἶος σὺν γαμβροῖσι κασιγνήτοισί τε σοῖσι.
sentences.tr:
phēs pou ater laōn polin hexemen ēd’ epikourōn
oios syn gambroisi kasignētoisi te soisi.
sentences.l:
You say, I suppose, that without the people and the allies the city you will hold,
alone, with brothers-in-law and with your brothers.
sentences.i: You say, I suppose, that you will hold the city without troops and allies, alone, with your brothers-in-law and your brothers.
sentences.n: φῆς που is ‘you say, I suppose’ (που softens the claim). ἑξέμεν is the future infinitive of ἔχω with the epic ending -έμεν, ‘will hold’. ἄτερ ‘without’ takes the genitives λαῶν and ἐπικούρων; ἐπίκουροι are ‘allies’, the troops from outside Troy who fight for Priam, of whom Sarpedon is one. οἶος ‘alone’ and σὺν γαμβροῖσι κασιγνήτοισί τε σοῖσι ‘with brothers-in-law and your brothers’: γαμβρός means any man related by marriage (son-in-law, brother-in-law), and here the men who have married into Hector’s family.

sentences.t:
τῶν νῦν οὔ τιν’ ἐγὼ ἰδέειν δύναμ’ οὐδὲ νοῆσαι,
ἀλλὰ καταπτώσσουσι κύνες ὣς ἀμφὶ λέοντα·
sentences.tr:
tōn nyn ou tin’ egō ideein dynam’ oude noēsai,
alla kataptōssousi kynes hōs amphi leonta·
sentences.l:
Of these now not one can I see or notice,
but they cower, like dogs around a lion;
sentences.i: I cannot now see or notice any one of them, but they cower like dogs around a lion;
sentences.n: τῶν … τιν’ is ‘any one of these’, Hector’s kin. ἰδέειν and νοῆσαι are aorist infinitives (the first with the epic ending -έειν), ‘see’ and ‘notice’, and δύναμ’ is δύναμαι ‘I am able’ with its final vowel elided. καταπτώσσουσι is ‘they cower’ (καταπτώσσω); κύνες ὣς ἀμφὶ λέοντα is ‘like dogs around a lion’, with ὥς ‘like’ placed after the noun it goes with. Sarpedon says that not one of Hector’s kin is to be seen fighting.

sentences.t: ἡμεῖς δὲ μαχόμεσθ’ οἵ πέρ τ’ ἐπίκουροι ἔνειμεν.
sentences.tr: hēmeis de machomesth’ hoi per t’ epikouroi eneimen.
sentences.l: But we are fighting, we who are only allies here.
sentences.i: It is we who fight, we who are only allies among you.
sentences.n: ἡμεῖς δέ ‘but we’ stresses the contrast with the kin of Hector. μαχόμεσθ’ is μαχόμεσθα, the first person plural middle of μάχομαι with its final vowel elided. οἵ πέρ τ’ ἐπίκουροι ἔνειμεν is ‘we who are only allies’: πέρ (‘just, even’) and the epic τε give the clause the sense ‘we, allies as we are’; ἔνειμεν is ἔνεσμεν, the first person plural of εἰμί with the preverb ἐν- ‘be in, be here’ (εἰμέν is the epic form of ἐσμέν).

sentences.t: καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼν ἐπίκουρος ἐὼν μάλα τηλόθεν ἥκω·
sentences.tr: kai gar egōn epikouros eōn mala tēlothen hēkō·
sentences.l: For I too, being an ally, have come from very far away;
sentences.i: For I too am an ally, and I have come from very far away;
sentences.n: καὶ γὰρ ἐγών is ‘for I too’; ἐγών is a by-form of ἐγώ, and ἐπίκουρος ἐών is ‘being an ally’, ἐών the epic participle of εἰμί (Attic ὤν). τηλόθεν is ‘from afar’ (the suffix -θεν marks ‘from’), and ἥκω ‘I have come’ is a present with the sense of a perfect.

sentences.t:
τηλοῦ γὰρ Λυκίη Ξάνθῳ ἔπι δινήεντι,
ἔνθ’ ἄλοχόν τε φίλην ἔλιπον καὶ νήπιον υἱόν,
κὰδ δὲ κτήματα πολλά, τὰ ἔλδεται ὅς κ’ ἐπιδευής.
sentences.tr:
tēlou gar Lykiē Xanthōi epi dinēenti,
enth’ alochon te philēn elipon kai nēpion huion,
kad de ktēmata polla, ta eldetai hos k’ epideuēs.
sentences.i: For Lycia is far away, by the eddying Xanthus, where I left my dear wife and my little son, and many possessions, such as a man in need longs for.
sentences.n: τηλοῦ γάρ ‘for far away’ explains the long journey. Λυκίη is Lycia, the subject of an unstated ‘is’; Ξάνθῳ ἔπι δινήεντι is ‘beside the eddying Xanthus’, with ἔπι placed after its noun, and δινήεις ‘eddying’ (δίνη ‘eddy’) is the river’s epithet, as in the Catalogue (2.877). ἔνθ’ ἄλοχόν τε φίλην ἔλιπον καὶ νήπιον υἱόν is ‘where I left my dear wife and my infant son’ (ἔλιπον, the aorist of λείπω; νήπιος is here ‘infant’, a child too young to speak, and elsewhere ‘foolish’). κὰδ δέ is κατὰ δέ, with κατά in tmesis (‘left behind’) its last vowel dropped and its τ made δ before the following δ. κτήματα is ‘possessions’; τά ‘which’ is the article as a relative; ἔλδεται is ‘longs for’ (ἔλδομαι); and ὅς κ’ ἐπιδευής is ‘whoever is in want’, a general relative with ἐπιδευής ‘lacking’ and its verb understood.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς Λυκίους ὀτρύνω καὶ μέμον’ αὐτὸς
ἀνδρὶ μαχήσασθαι·
sentences.tr:
alla kai hōs Lykious otrynō kai memon’ autos
andri machēsasthai·
sentences.l:
But even so I urge on the Lycians, and am myself eager
to fight a man;
sentences.i: But even so I urge on the Lycians, and I am eager myself to fight a man;
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς is ‘but even so’ (ὥς ‘thus’). ὀτρύνω is the present, ‘I urge on’; μέμον’ is μέμονα (a perfect with present sense) ‘I am eager’, with its final vowel elided, and αὐτός ‘myself’ marks that Sarpedon does the fighting himself. ἀνδρὶ μαχήσασθαι is ‘to fight a man’, the aorist infinitive of μάχομαι with the dative; the man is any man who comes.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ οὔ τί μοι ἐνθάδε τοῖον
οἷόν κ’ ἠὲ φέροιεν Ἀχαιοὶ ἤ κεν ἄγοιεν·
sentences.tr:
atar ou ti moi enthade toion
hoion k’ ēe pheroien Achaioi ē ken agoien·
sentences.l:
but not at all is there for me here such a thing
as the Achaeans might either carry off or bring away;
sentences.i: but I have nothing here of the sort the Achaeans could carry off or bring away;
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘but’ brings in the point: at Troy he has nothing for the enemy to take. οὔ τί μοι ἐνθάδε τοῖον … οἷον is ‘nothing of mine here of the kind that’, τοῖον … οἷον ‘such … as’, and κε(ν) with the optatives φέροιεν and ἄγοιεν gives ‘might’; ἠέ … ἤ is ‘either … or’. The pair φέρειν and ἄγειν is the pair for plunder, things carried and animals or people brought away.

sentences.t:
τύνη δ’ ἕστηκας, ἀτὰρ οὐδ’ ἄλλοισι κελεύεις
λαοῖσιν μενέμεν καὶ ἀμυνέμεναι ὤρεσσι.
sentences.tr:
tynē d’ hestēkas, atar oud’ alloisi keleueis
laoisin menemen kai amynemenai ōressi.
sentences.l:
But you yourself stand still, and not even to the other peoples do you bid
to stay and to ward off for their wives.
sentences.i: But you just stand there, and you do not even bid the other troops to hold their ground and ward off harm for their wives.
sentences.n: τύνη is the emphatic epic form of σύ (‘you yourself’), and ἕστηκας is the perfect of ἵστημι with present sense, ‘you stand’. ἀτὰρ οὐδ’ is ‘and not even’. κελεύεις takes the dative ἄλλοισι λαοῖσιν ‘the other troops’ and two infinitives with the epic endings -έμεν and -έμεναι, μενέμεν ‘to stay, hold firm’ and ἀμυνέμεναι ‘to ward off’, which has no object in the Greek (‘harm’ is supplied in the English). ὤρεσσι is the dative plural of ὄαρ ‘wife’, ‘(for) their wives’, the usual explanation of this rare word.

sentences.t:
μή πως ὡς ἀψῖσι λίνου ἁλόντε πανάγρου
ἀνδράσι δυσμενέεσσιν ἕλωρ καὶ κύρμα γένησθε·
sentences.tr:
mē pōs hōs apsisi linou halonte panagrou
andrasi dysmeneessin helōr kai kyrma genēsthe·
sentences.l:
lest somehow, as if in the meshes of an all-catching net of flax having been caught, the two of you
to hostile men prey and spoil may become;
sentences.i: lest the two of you, caught as if in the meshes of an all-catching net of flax, become prey and spoil for hostile men;
sentences.n: μή πως ὡς … γένησθε is a warning, ‘lest somehow … you become’: μή with the aorist subjunctive. ἁλόντε is the dual aorist participle of ἁλίσκομαι ‘be caught’, ‘the two of you caught’, yet the verb γένησθε is plural; who the two are the Greek does not say, and the English keeps the dual. ἀψῖσι is the dative plural of ἁψίς, the loops or meshes of a net; λίνου ‘of flax’ names its stuff, and πανάγρου ‘all-catching’ (πᾶν + ἄγρα ‘catch’) its power. ἕλωρ ‘prey’ and κύρμα ‘spoil’ (something chanced upon) are a pair of near-synonyms, translated as two words, as in the Odyssey’s ἕλωρ καὶ κύρμα (3.271, ‘prey and spoil’); δυσμενέεσσιν ‘hostile’ is the epic dative plural of δυσμενής.

sentences.t: οἳ δὲ τάχ’ ἐκπέρσουσ’ εὖ ναιομένην πόλιν ὑμήν.
sentences.tr: hoi de tach’ ekpersous’ eu naiomenēn polin hymēn.
sentences.l: and they soon will sack the well-inhabited city of yours.
sentences.i: and they will soon sack your well-inhabited city.
sentences.n: οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the hostile men. ἐκπέρσουσ’ is the future of ἐκπέρθω ‘sack’, ἐκπέρσουσι with its final -ι lost before the vowel, and τάχα ‘soon’. εὖ ναιομένην ‘well-inhabited’ is the passive participle of ναίω ‘dwell’, a stock phrase for a city; ὑμήν is the feminine accusative of ὑμός, an epic form of ὑμέτερος ‘your’ (plural), so the city is the Trojans’ own, the one Hector leads, not the allies’.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δὲ χρὴ τάδε πάντα μέλειν νύκτάς τε καὶ ἦμαρ
ἀρχοὺς λισσομένῳ τηλεκλειτῶν ἐπικούρων
νωλεμέως ἐχέμεν, κρατερὴν δ’ ἀποθέσθαι ἐνιπήν.
sentences.tr:
soi de chrē tade panta melein nyktas te kai ēmar
archous lissomenōi tēlekleitōn epikourōn
nōlemeōs echemen, kraterēn d’ apothesthai enipēn.
sentences.l:
On you it is necessary that all this be a care, by night and by day,
entreating the leaders of the far-famed allies
to hold firm unceasingly, and to lay aside strong rebuke.”
sentences.i: It is for you to take thought for all this, night and day, begging the leaders of the far-famed allies to hold firm without pause and to lay aside their strong rebuke.”
sentences.n: σοὶ δὲ χρὴ … μέλειν is ‘you must take care of’ (literally ‘it is necessary that for you … be a care’): χρή with the infinitive μέλειν, whose subject is τάδε πάντα ‘all this’, and the dative σοί. νύκτας τε καὶ ἦμαρ is ‘night and day’, accusatives of time. λισσομένῳ is a dative participle agreeing with σοί, ‘begging’, with the accusative ἀρχούς ‘leaders’ (ἀρχός ‘commander’) as the men begged, and the two infinitives ἐχέμεν ‘to hold firm’ and ἀποθέσθαι ‘to lay aside’ saying what they are begged to do; νωλεμέως ‘unceasingly’ (‘without pause’ in the English) goes with ἐχέμεν. τηλεκλειτῶν ‘far-famed’ (τηλε- ‘far’ + κλειτός ‘famed’) belongs to the allies; κρατερὴν … ἐνιπήν is ‘strong rebuke’. The construction is compressed and the Greek does not say whose rebuke is meant; the English follows the plain grammar, so that it is the leaders who put it aside. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο Σαρπηδών, δάκε δὲ φρένας Ἕκτορι μῦθος·
sentences.tr: hōs phato Sarpēdōn, dake de phrenas Hektori mythos·
sentences.l: So spoke Sarpedon, and bit in the wits Hector the speech;
sentences.i: So spoke Sarpedon, and his words bit into Hector’s wits;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο Σαρπηδών ‘so spoke Sarpedon’ closes the speech. δάκε is the aorist of δάκνω ‘bite’, with μῦθος ‘speech’ as its subject; φρένας ‘wits’ (φρένες, the seat of understanding and feeling) is the part affected, and Ἕκτορι is the dative of the person, so ‘bit Hector in his wits’. A new paragraph begins at 493.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ἐξ ὀχέων σὺν τεύχεσιν ἆλτο χαμᾶζε,
πάλλων δ’ ὀξέα δοῦρα κατὰ στρατὸν ᾤχετο πάντῃ
ὀτρύνων μαχέσασθαι, ἔγειρε δὲ φύλοπιν αἰνήν.
sentences.tr:
autika d’ ex ocheōn syn teuchesin alto chamaze,
pallōn d’ oxea doura kata straton ōicheto pantēi
otrynōn machesasthai, egeire de phylopin ainēn.
sentences.l:
and at once from the chariot, with his armour, he leapt to the ground,
and brandishing sharp spears he went through the army everywhere,
urging them to fight, and he roused fearsome battle-din.
sentences.i: and at once he leapt from his chariot to the ground in his armour, and brandishing sharp spears he went everywhere through the army, urging the men to fight, and he roused fearsome battle-din.
sentences.n: The subject is Hector, and the first line is the line that tells of Menelaus’ leap at 3.29; the English is that one. ἆλτο is the aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’, χαμᾶζε is ‘to the ground’ (the suffix -ζε = -δε marks direction), and ὀχέων is a plural for the one chariot. πάλλων is ‘brandishing’ (πάλλω ‘shake’); ὀξέα δοῦρα are ‘sharp spears’ (δόρυ, plural δοῦρα); κατὰ στρατόν is ‘through the army’; ᾤχετο is the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘go’; πάντῃ is ‘everywhere’. ὀτρύνων μαχέσασθαι is ‘urging to fight’ (aorist infinitive of μάχομαι). ἔγειρε is the imperfect of ἐγείρω ‘rouse’ without the augment, with φύλοπιν αἰνήν ‘fearsome battle-din’, a stock phrase.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἐλελίχθησαν καὶ ἐναντίοι ἔσταν Ἀχαιῶν·
Ἀργεῖοι δ’ ὑπέμειναν ἀολλέες οὐδὲ φόβηθεν.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ elelichthēsan kai enantioi estan Achaiōn·
Argeioi d’ hypemeinan aollees oude phobēthen.
sentences.l:
And they were whirled round and stood opposite the Achaeans;
but the Argives stood their ground, in a close mass, and were not put to flight.
sentences.i: They wheeled round and took their stand facing the Achaeans, and the Argives held their ground in a close mass and did not take flight.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ is ‘and they’, the Trojans whom Hector has roused, set against Ἀργεῖοι ‘Argives’, the Achaeans under another name. ἐλελίχθησαν is the aorist passive of ἐλελίζω ‘whirl, make quiver’ (the verb of 1.530), ‘were whirled round’, that is, wheeled round. ἐναντίοι … Ἀχαιῶν is ‘facing the Achaeans’, and ἔσταν is ἔστησαν, an intransitive aorist, ‘took their stand’. ὑπέμειναν is ‘stood their ground’ (ὑπομένω), ἀολλέες ‘in a close mass’ (ἀολλής ‘crowded together’), and φόβηθεν the aorist passive of φοβέομαι with the epic ending -θεν for -θησαν, ‘took flight’; in battle φόβος is the running that fear drives.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ἄνεμος ἄχνας φορέει ἱερὰς κατ’ ἀλωὰς
ἀνδρῶν λικμώντων, ὅτε τε ξανθὴ Δημήτηρ
κρίνῃ ἐπειγομένων ἀνέμων καρπόν τε καὶ ἄχνας,
αἳ δ’ ὑπολευκαίνονται ἀχυρμιαί·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ anemos achnas phoreei hieras kat’ alōas
andrōn likmōntōn, hote te xanthē Dēmētēr
krinēi epeigomenōn anemōn karpon te kai achnas,
hai d’ hypoleukainontai achyrmiai·
sentences.l:
And as the wind carries chaff over the sacred threshing-floors
of men winnowing, when fair-haired Demeter
sorts, as the winds press on, grain and chaff,
and the chaff-heaps grow white beneath;
sentences.i: As the wind carries chaff over the sacred threshing-floors while men winnow, when fair-haired Demeter sorts grain and chaff as the winds press on, and the heaps of chaff grow white beneath;
sentences.n: A simile, begun by ὡς δ’ ‘and as’, picks up the dust of the battle; its second half, ὣς τότ’, is in the next unit. ἄνεμος ἄχνας φορέει is ‘the wind carries chaff’ (present, because the simile states what always happens), ἱερὰς κατ’ ἀλωάς ‘over the sacred threshing-floors’: ἀλωή is a threshing-floor here (elsewhere a cultivated plot, an orchard at 5.90). ἀνδρῶν λικμώντων is a genitive absolute, ‘men winnowing’ (λικμάω ‘winnow’). ὅτε τε … κρίνῃ is ‘when … sorts’ (κρίνω ‘sort’, as at 2.362), general, with the subjunctive; ξανθή ‘fair-haired’ is the Odyssey’s epithet, and ξανθὴ Δημήτηρ is Demeter, the goddess of grain, named as the power at work in the winnowing. ἐπειγομένων ἀνέμων ‘as the winds press on’ is another genitive absolute; καρπόν is the grain and ἄχνας the chaff. αἳ δ’ ὑπολευκαίνονται ἀχυρμιαί is ‘and the chaff-heaps grow white beneath’ (ἀχυρμιά ‘heap of chaff’).

sentences.t:
ὣς τότ’ Ἀχαιοὶ
λευκοὶ ὕπερθε γένοντο κονισάλῳ, ὅν ῥα δι’ αὐτῶν
οὐρανὸν ἐς πολύχαλκον ἐπέπληγον πόδες ἵππων
ἂψ ἐπιμισγομένων·
sentences.tr:
hōs tot’ Achaioi
leukoi hyperthe genonto konisalōi, hon rha di’ autōn
ouranon es polychalkon epeplēgon podes hippōn
aps epimisgomenōn·
sentences.l:
so then the Achaeans
became white on top with the dust, which through them
into the sky of much bronze the feet of horses beat up,
as they mingled again;
sentences.i: so the Achaeans then became white on top with the dust that the feet of the horses beat up through their ranks into the sky of much bronze as the horses mingled again;
sentences.n: ὣς τότ’ is the second half of the simile: ‘so then the Achaeans’ means that they turn white as the heaps do. λευκοὶ ὕπερθε γένοντο κονισάλῳ is ‘became white on top with dust’ (γένοντο, the aorist of γίγνομαι without the augment; κονίσαλος ‘cloud of dust’, a dative of means). ὅν ῥα δι’ αὐτῶν is the relative ὅν (the dust) with ‘through them’; οὐρανὸν ἐς πολύχαλκον is ‘into the sky of much bronze’, the Odyssey’s phrase for a sky that is a bronze vault. ἐπέπληγον is the reduplicated aorist of ἐπιπλήσσω ‘strike upon’, here ‘beat up’; πόδες ἵππων ‘the feet of horses’ are the hooves, and ἂψ ἐπιμισγομένων ‘as they mingled again’ is a genitive going with ἵππων (ἐπιμίσγομαι ‘mingle with’, ἂψ ‘back, again’).

sentences.t: ὑπὸ δ’ ἔστρεφον ἡνιοχῆες.
sentences.tr: hypo d’ estrephon hēniochēes.
sentences.l: and beneath the charioteers were turning them about.
sentences.i: while beneath, the charioteers wheeled them about.
sentences.n: ὑπὸ δ’ ἔστρεφον ἡνιοχῆες has no object in the Greek; the horses (or chariots) are understood, and ‘them’ is supplied in the English. ἔστρεφον is the imperfect of στρέφω ‘turn’, and ἡνιοχῆες is the epic plural of ἡνιοχεύς, the same word as ἡνίοχος ‘charioteer’ (ἡνία ‘reins’ + ἔχω ‘hold’). ὑπό is read as ‘beneath’, which places the scene below the cloud of dust; it could also be tmesis for ὑποστρέφω ‘turn about’, and the Greek says no more.

sentences.t: οἳ δὲ μένος χειρῶν ἰθὺς φέρον·
sentences.tr: hoi de menos cheirōn ithys pheron·
sentences.l: And they bore the might of their hands straight on;
sentences.i: And they carried the might of their hands straight forward;
sentences.n: οἳ δέ ‘and they’ takes up the fighters again after the simile. μένος χειρῶν ‘the might of their hands’ is the force of their blows; ἰθύς ‘straight’ is an adverb; φέρον is the imperfect of φέρω without the augment. The ano teleia after φέρον sets this clause apart from what Ares does next.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δὲ νύκτα
θοῦρος Ἄρης ἐκάλυψε μάχῃ Τρώεσσιν ἀρήγων
πάντοσ’ ἐποιχόμενος·
sentences.tr:
amphi de nykta
thouros Arēs ekalypse machēi Trōessin arēgōn
pantos’ epoichomenos·
sentences.i: and impetuous Ares enfolded the battle in night, helping the Trojans as he went about everywhere;
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ δὲ νύκτα … ἐκάλυψε is tmesis for ἀμφεκάλυψε ‘enfolded’ (the verb of ἀμφικαλύπτω ‘enfold’, as at 5.68): the god wraps the fighting in night, and the Greek makes night the accusative, νύκτα, and the battle the dative, μάχῃ, which the freer English turns round. μάχῃ is a dative, ‘over the battle’ or ‘in the battle’. θοῦρος Ἄρης is the stock ‘impetuous Ares’ (454). Τρώεσσιν ἀρήγων is ‘helping the Trojans’ (ἀρήγω ‘help’), and πάντοσ’ ἐποιχόμενος ‘going about everywhere’ (πάντοσε ‘on every side’ with its final vowel elided; ἐποίχομαι ‘go about’). He acts at Apollo’s bidding, as the next unit says.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἐκραίαινεν ἐφετμὰς
Φοίβου Ἀπόλλωνος χρυσαόρου, ὅς μιν ἀνώγει
Τρωσὶν θυμὸν ἐγεῖραι, ἐπεὶ ἴδε Παλλάδ’ Ἀθήνην
οἰχομένην·
sentences.tr:
tou d’ ekraiainen ephetmas
Phoibou Apollōnos chrysaorou, hos min anōgei
Trōsin thymon egeirai, epei ide Pallad’ Athēnēn
oichomenēn·
sentences.l:
and his commands he was fulfilling,
of Phoebus Apollo of the golden sword, who bade him
rouse the heart for the Trojans, when he saw Pallas Athena
going away;
sentences.i: fulfilling the commands of Phoebus Apollo of the golden sword, who had bidden him rouse the hearts of the Trojans when he saw Pallas Athena going away;
sentences.n: τοῦ is Apollo (‘his’), and with its noun ἐφετμάς ‘commands’ it is the object of ἐκραίαινεν, the imperfect of κραιαίνω ‘bring to fulfilment’. Φοίβου Ἀπόλλωνος χρυσαόρου ‘of Phoebus Apollo of the golden sword’ is in apposition to τοῦ, and χρυσάωρ means ‘with a golden sword’ (χρυσός + ἄορ ‘sword’), a stock epithet translated every time. ὅς μιν ἀνώγει is ‘who bade him’ (ἀνώγει, the imperfect of ἄνωγα ‘bid’, with μιν ‘him’, Ares), with the infinitive ἐγεῖραι ‘to rouse’ and θυμὸν Τρωσίν ‘heart for the Trojans’ (θυμός ‘heart’, a dative of interest). ἐπεὶ ἴδε Παλλάδ’ Ἀθήνην οἰχομένην is ‘when he saw Pallas Athena going away’ (ἴδε, the aorist of ὁράω without the augment; οἰχομένην, the participle of οἴχομαι ‘be gone’; Παλλάδ’, the accusative of Παλλάς, a title of Athena, elided).

sentences.t: ἣ γάρ ῥα πέλεν Δαναοῖσιν ἀρηγών.
sentences.tr: hē gar rha pelen Danaoisin arēgōn.
sentences.l: for she it was who was a helper to the Danaans.
sentences.i: for she was the helper of the Danaans.
sentences.n: ἣ γάρ ῥα is ‘for she, then’, and gives the reason Apollo chose this moment: Athena, the Danaans’ helper, had left the field. πέλεν is the imperfect of πέλομαι ‘be’ without the augment, and ἀρηγών is a noun, ‘helper’ (ἀρήγω ‘help’, as in Τρώεσσιν ἀρήγων above). Δαναοῖσιν is the dative of Δαναοί, the Danaans, one of the army’s three names.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ Αἰνείαν μάλα πίονος ἐξ ἀδύτοιο
ἧκε, καὶ ἐν στήθεσσι μένος βάλε ποιμένι λαῶν.
sentences.tr:
autos d’ Aineian mala pionos ex adytoio
hēke, kai en stēthessi menos bale poimeni laōn.
sentences.l:
And he himself Aeneas out of the very rich inner sanctuary
sent forth, and in his chest might cast for the shepherd of the people.
sentences.i: And he himself sent Aeneas out of the very rich inner sanctuary, and put might in the chest of the shepherd of the people.
sentences.n: αὐτὸς δ’ is ‘and he himself’, Apollo again. μάλα πίονος ‘very rich’ (πίων ‘fat, rich’; the Greek does not say rich in what) goes with ἐξ ἀδύτοιο ‘out of the inner sanctuary’ (see 448). ἧκε is the aorist of ἵημι ‘send’, with Αἰνείαν as its object: Apollo brings Aeneas back into the fight. ἐν στήθεσσι … βάλε is ‘put in his chest’, ἐν … βάλε being ἐνέβαλε in tmesis, with στήθεσσι the epic dative plural and μένος ‘might’. ποιμένι λαῶν ‘to the shepherd of the people’ is the stock phrase for a leader, here Aeneas, translated every time.

sentences.t: Αἰνείας δ’ ἑτάροισι μεθίστατο·
sentences.tr: Aineias d’ hetaroisi methistato·
sentences.l: And Aeneas took his stand among his companions;
sentences.i: Aeneas took his place among his companions;
sentences.n: μεθίστατο is the middle of μεθίστημι, here with the dative ‘take one’s stand among’, so ‘joined’; ἑτάροισι is the epic dative plural of ἑταῖρος ‘companion’. The ano teleia ends the clause, and the next shows how they received him.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δὲ χάρησαν,
ὡς εἶδον ζωόν τε καὶ ἀρτεμέα προσιόντα
καὶ μένος ἐσθλὸν ἔχοντα·
sentences.tr:
toi de charēsan,
hōs eidon zōon te kai artemea prosionta
kai menos esthlon echonta·
sentences.i: and they were glad when they saw him alive and unharmed, coming toward them, and with good might in him;
sentences.n: τοί is the article as a pronoun, ‘they’, his companions; χάρησαν is the aorist of χαίρω ‘be glad’, and ὡς εἶδον ‘when they saw’ (εἶδον, the aorist of ὁράω). ζωόν ‘alive’ is the epic adjective (Attic ζῶν), and ἀρτεμέα ‘unharmed’ (ἀρτεμής ‘sound, safe’). The participles προσιόντα ‘coming toward’ and ἔχοντα ‘having’ agree with the unstated ‘him’, Aeneas, the object of εἶδον. μένος ἐσθλόν ‘good might’ is the strength Apollo put into him at 513.

sentences.t: μετάλλησάν γε μὲν οὔ τι.
sentences.tr: metallēsan ge men ou ti.
sentences.l: but they questioned him not at all.
sentences.i: but they asked him nothing.
sentences.n: γε μέν ‘but yet’ turns the sentence round. μετάλλησαν is the aorist of μεταλλάω ‘ask, inquire’ (the object ‘him’ is understood), with οὔ τι ‘not at all’, so ‘asked nothing’. The next line says why.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔα πόνος ἄλλος, ὃν ἀργυρότοξος ἔγειρεν
Ἄρης τε βροτολοιγὸς Ἔρις τ’ ἄμοτον μεμαυῖα.
sentences.tr:
ou gar ea ponos allos, hon argyrotoxos egeiren
Arēs te brotoloigos Eris t’ amoton memauia.
sentences.l:
For did not allow another toil, which the silver-bowed one
roused, and mortal-ruining Ares, and Strife, unceasingly eager.
sentences.i: For the other toil did not allow it, the toil that the silver-bowed one had roused, and Ares, ruin of mortals, and Strife, eager without ceasing.
sentences.n: οὐ γὰρ ἔα πόνος ἄλλος explains the unit before: they asked nothing because another toil, the fighting, did not allow it (ἔα, the imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’, without the augment; πόνος ‘toil’). The relative clause ὃν … ἔγειρεν has three subjects for one singular verb (the imperfect of ἐγείρω ‘rouse’): ἀργυρότοξος ‘the silver-bowed one’, who is Apollo, though the Greek does not name him and ἀργυρότοξος is his stock epithet; Ἄρης … βροτολοιγός ‘Ares, ruin of mortals’ (see 455); and Ἔρις ‘Strife’, the personified power of conflict, capitalised in English as a being. ἄμοτον μεμαυῖα ‘eager without ceasing’ (ἄμοτον ‘unceasingly’ is an adverb whose exact sense is not known; μεμαυῖα is the feminine participle of μέμονα ‘be eager’) is the phrase used of Strife at 4.440.
